passage: I'm Karthik, Asif's classmate, and I was at his flat on Saturday doing our project when his father knocked. "Text me when you reach the library. And wear the helmet, please." Asif answered without looking up. "Papa, nobody does that anymore." After the door closed he muttered, "Stuck in the nineties. He thinks the road is a war zone." He picked up his phone and read a message out loud in a silly voice: "Take the jacket, it's cold." Then he stopped, and I saw him look at the closed door. "His friend had an accident once," he said quietly. "That's why." He put on the jacket anyway. I honestly can't tell whether he was more annoyed or worried.

qa.q: What did Asif's father ask him to do when he reached the library?
qa.a: He asked him to text when he reached the library.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling when he stopped mocking the message and looked at the closed door?
qa.a: Possibly a flicker of understanding, since he mentioned his father's friend's accident, though Karthik admits he can't tell if Asif was more annoyed or worried.

qa.q: What could Asif try next time his father sets a rule like this?
qa.a: He could keep his father's worry in mind while suggesting an easier way to check in, so they can talk about the fear and not just the method.

qa.q: How might Asif's father feel when his son sneers at the rule?
qa.a: Possibly hurt or brushed aside, even though the rule comes from fear for his son's safety.

grounding: Shows a teen sneering at his father's rules as outdated, an observer seeing him briefly separate the fear behind the rule from the method.

qa.q: Which camp did Farida's parents refuse?
What does Farida's comment about Abba and email show about her attitude?
qa.a: She is frustrated and scornful, starting to see her parents as backward so their words stop counting.

qa.q: What wiser step did Tenzin suggest?

grounding: A teenager starts treating her parents as backward and clueless, and a friend helps her separate their fear from their methods and hear the concern.

passage:
Pankaj's father had said no again. "The highway to Jalgaon is dangerous. Take the bus."
"The bus takes three hours, Baba! You don't even know how anything works now," Pankaj snapped. Then, under his breath, to his cousin Pranav: "Village thinking. They still believe the radio is the internet."
Pranav, who had just got his licence, didn't laugh. "Your Baba lost his friend Suresh on that highway, remember? He's not stupid. He's scared."
Pankaj went quiet. He had forgotten Suresh Kaka.
That evening he sat beside Baba on the charpai. "Baba, I spoke rudely. I still think the bus is too slow. What if I go pillion with Pranav, both of us in helmets, and never after dark?"
Baba looked out at the dark field for a long time. "Show me the helmets first."

qa.q: Which friend of Baba's died on the highway?
What was behind Pankaj's "village thinking" remark?
qa.a: Frustration turning into contempt; he was seeing Baba as clueless so his words stopped counting.

qa.q: How did Pankaj move from sneering to a wiser approach?
qa.a: He apologised for being rude and proposed a safer plan that answered Baba's actual fear.

qa.q: How does Baba likely see the highway?
qa.a: As a real danger, because he lost his friend Suresh on it.

grounding: A teenager begins to sneer at his father as backward, then separates the father's fear from his old-fashioned ways and hears the concern.
